title: Mentally ill man put up fierce battle before arrest, fatality inquiry is told: Taser gun seen as possible aid in case
article: The use of a taser stun gun rather than pepper spray may have better subdued a mentally ill man police were struggling with, a fatality inquiry heard Friday.
Kasim Cakmak died last May 11 after resisting arrest, being pepper sprayed and handcuffed when police were called to the downtown mental health outpatient clinic at 9942 108th St.
They had been asked to transport Cakmak to Alberta Hospital Edmonton because the paranoid schizophrenic had been acting aggressively at a recreation program at the clinic.

When approached by a male psychiatric nurse and two police officers in a room on the fourth floor, Cakmak resisted and a great struggle ensued for about 10 minutes. "In my 30 years I've never seen anybody react as bad before," said psychiatric nurse Romona Levesque.
Const. Trudy Triplett, arrest and control instructor with the Edmonton Police Service's training section, told the inquiry both police officers acted properly and did not use excessive force.
She speculated that the use of a taser, an electronic immobilizing device, may have worked better than pepper spray to subdue Cakmak. "The incident may have had the same result, it may not have."

Alberta's chief medical examiner earlier testified that Cakmak died from excited delirium, a rare condition in which extreme agitation creates an adrenalin rush that stops the heart. He said he doubted that pepper spray contributed to his death.
Const. Scott Innes testified Friday that when he and Const. John Tedeschini initially approached Cakmak, he was sitting in a chair at a table, clenching his fists, moaning and grunting.
When psychiatric nurse Mike Brohman told Cakmak the police were going to take him to Alberta Hospital, he became agitated.
The police approached him from both sides and tried to bring his arms back to handcuff him.
But he easily pulled his hands away, said Innes, who then decided to get him down on the floor. When he and Cakmak fell over the chair, Cakmak became extremely aggressive.
"I tried to hold onto his arm but I couldn't," said Innes. "We rolled him over on his stomach and continued to struggle. It was a fairly high level of intensity. I was getting tired."
After giving Cakmak two blows to the head with his open palm to no effect, Innes called for more police backup on his radio.
Tedeschini then decided to use the pepper spray, spraying Cakmak in the face. "It had no effect at all," said Innes.
Innes then gave him two or three blows with his knee to his abdomen. That had no effect, so he punched him twice in the back of the head with a closed fist. Again, no effect.
Cakmak had grabbed onto the table leg and Innes tried with all his strength to get him to release his grip.

Then he took out his collapsible baton and applied pressure to the back of his ear, which was effective. After using the baton to apply pressure to Cakmak's wrist, the pair were able to handcuff him. Then Brohman noticed Cakmak was turning blue, so they sat him up and removed the handcuffs.

When no pulse was found, Brohman started cardio-pulmonary resuscitation, which was continued by another police officer, a former nurse, who arrived later at the scene. Then paramedics took over and Cakmak was taken to hospital.
Triplett said she's concerned with the increasing number of calls police get about mentally ill people. Last year police responded to more than 1,000 such calls, she said.
